The project

The lands of the Ligurian-Emilian hinterland are not living through the most glorious moment in their history. Lured by the better material conditions of the cities, people leave, abandoning for ever the places of their forebears.

And so the villages empty. The inns and taverns close. Communities break up and ancient knowledge vanishes. Mountain farming and shepherding are set aside. The old houses collapse. The ancient mule tracks are overrun by weeds and made unusable. In other words, the Apennines and their thousand-year-old civilisation, squeezed between the hyper-tourism of the Riviera and the hyper-industrialisation of the plains, are being eroded by the slow but relentless action of abandonment and oblivion.

One might delude oneself that, at least, the silence and the void left by humankind herald the return of a pristine nature. But not even this is entirely true. Climate change and the impact of certain human activities are shattering ecosystems, which are in turn under the pressure of worsening air quality and a progressive loss of habitat. The extent of the rift between the landscape and its inhabitants can be savoured by wandering along the beds of the torrents, the gorges and the valleys, often filled with rubbish accumulated over the decades, itself the sign of an industrial civilisation capable of regenerating itself, but not of disposing of itself.

It would be wishful thinking to believe that the mere rediscovery of the Antica Via del Cifalco could stop this haemorrhage; yet the fortunate walkers who will have the privilege of travelling it will be offered an opportunity to reflect on how to halt – at least in their own conscience – this short circuit that afflicts the perception of our environment, our landscape, our roots.

In the wake of this tacit and discreet urge to rebel, the Antica Via del Cifalco project has brought a legendary road back to light. Over about 75 kilometres (not counting the many possible detours), and running along the entire Trebbia-Aveto ridge, it leads from the emerald-coloured waters of the river Trebbia near Ponte Organasco (in the province of Piacenza, Emilia-Romagna) to the coast of the Levante Ligure (in the province of Genoa, Liguria).

The Antica Via del Cifalco is more than just a path. It is a holistic project whose main aims are to:

  • Enhance a route travelled for centuries by merchants, monks, brigands, soldiers, vagabonds and travelling performers, and carrying a priceless wealth of history, legends and local culture, allowing travellers to rediscover a sense of wonder and encouraging them to take a poetic and mindful look at the places that unfold before them.
  • Prompt reflection on the decline of peasant civilisation and on the issues linked to rural development and mountain depopulation, passing through charming villages and immersing oneself for days in a natural world that remains unique for the richness and variety of its flora, fauna and ecosystems.
  • Make a concrete contribution to safeguarding the economic activities of the people who, just like resistance fighters, keep the territory alive. All of them deserve our gratitude: it is only thanks to this heroic work that the Antica Via del Cifalco can boast places to eat (well), to spend the night and to enjoy moments of exchange and learning.

To do this, our project has drawn on no funding or financial contribution of any kind, either public or private. It was carried out through the efforts and at the expense of its creator, who acted solely on a voluntary basis. It pursues no profit and no political aims going beyond raising awareness of the issues mentioned above.

The people

Luchino Ferraris is the creator and rediscoverer of the Antica Via del Cifalco, as well as the author of the pages of this site. There would be little point in trying to preserve his anonymity. Nonetheless, he does not feel he needs to add anything else about himself: the conception of this project and its realisation speak of him sufficiently.

Alongside him, the Compagnia del Cifalco operates as an informal and spontaneous group of people – representatives of public administrations, operators and other volunteers – who have contributed decisively to the success of the project and continue to do so.

It is open to new adepts! Please note, however, that this is not a list of sympathisers, but of people who make a concrete and effective contribution to the cause.

We did not invent the Antica Via del Cifalco: it already existed, buried beneath an ocean of indifference. We would like to hope that other people, on coming into contact with our project, will be seized by the urgency of memory and by the need to create value.

Acknowledgements

First of all, we wish to thank the Administration of Cerignale, in particular in the person of the Deputy Mayor Marco Besozzi, who from the very start did his utmost to help us. In a way, our gratitude extends to all the local administrations of the 17 Municipalities crossed by the path, both those that supported the project and also those that, at the very least, chose not to boycott it, or tried to without succeeding.

Projects succeed if they are well conceived, but then they need passionate and dedicated people who are ready to make room among the commitments of their lives in order to get their hands dirty on the ground. Among them, Gianni de Billio, Stefano Privitera and Paola Terzi deserve our deepest gratitude. Without them, it would have been impossible to bring back to life long stretches of the path network, especially between M. Caucaso and M. di Portofino. They are the true hoplites of the Via del Cifalco and, by now, friends as well.

Thanks also to my friend Giuliano Ferretti of the Trattoria del Valico di Fregarolo, who on a stormy afternoon welcomed like a king an unknown wayfarer at the mercy of the blizzard, feeding him beside a stove and sharing with him deep knowledge of the things of the world.

Alongside these protagonists, we also wish to express our thanks to:

  • Pietro Nigelli, essential for coordinating the path network, in particular on the Emilian side (but not only there), and a true guru of Apennine hiking, including through his association Appennino Trekking.
  • Giorgio de Angelis, President of the Pro Loco of Cerignale.
  • Sandro Sbarbaro, Giorgio Castignoli and Giacomo Bracchi, without whose suggestions the historical and naturalistic parts of the site would be decidedly less authoritative. It has been an honour to benefit from their absolutely first-rate knowledge of the most hidden nuances of our territory. Sandro runs that priceless goldmine of knowledge that is the website Valdaveto.net, and Giacomo leads the successful Facebook group Il mio Appennino.
  • Fabrizio Capecchi, friend and mentor, from whom I first heard of the existence of the Antica Via del Cifalco.
  • Fabrizio Bottari, another of Fabrizio Capecchi’s disciples, himself the author of important texts on the territory and founder of an International Potato Museum not to be missed if you find yourself on the “other” side of Val d’Aveto from the Via del Cifalco. Fabrizio is also the guardian spirit of the Foundation that safeguards the integrity of the Bosco Fontana, a beech forest of about 300 hectares occupying the basin of the Rezzoaglio torrent, on the northern slope of M. Aiona.
  • Giuseppe Noroni of Nomad Geography, former President of the Via degli Abati, and our cartographer.
  • Emanuele Roccatagliata, of the Genoa section of the Federazione Italiana Escursionisti (FIE) and manager of the website https://www.roccatagliata.eu, generous with valuable advice and practical help on hiking matters.
  • Giancarlo Alimonti and Daniela Possenti, who deserve the credit for designing our logo and signage, and who must be honoured for the patience with which they endured the countless exchanges over the various intermediate drafts.
  • Alessandra Mazzilli, to whose creativity, taste and technical skills we owe our wonderful website!
